records.title: Three men. One ground test.
records.dek: This was a ground test, not a launch. The rocket was unfueled; the spacecraft was not free of danger.
records.detail: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee prepared for the Plugs-Out Test at Launch Complex 34. The test had not been classified as hazardous because only tests involving fueled vehicles were, and the launch vehicle was unfueled. The spacecraft still held a 100 percent oxygen atmosphere, combustible materials and an innermost hatch that took 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions.
records.caution: An unfueled launch vehicle did not mean a safe cabin.

image.alt: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee standing near Launch Complex 34 during training in January 1967.
image.caption: The Apollo 1 crew near Launch Complex 34 during training, January 1967.
image.identity_note: The NASA record page "Apollo 1 Crew Honored" gives the caption and credit; the identifier appears in the image file name on that page. The copy is served from the Final Vestige media library.

crosswalk.claim: The January 27, 1967 Plugs-Out Test was run with the launch vehicle unfueled.
crosswalk.source: NASA History (2022): "Because the test took place with the rocket unfueled, it had been considered non-hazardous". Board report, Part IV: the Plugs-Out Test was not classified as hazardous because only tests involving fueled vehicles were.

crosswalk.claim: The innermost hatch took 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions.
crosswalk.source: NASA History (2022): the innermost hatch opened inward "and taking 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions".

records.title: An atmosphere built for a different risk.
records.dek: One hundred percent oxygen at elevated ground-test pressure greatly increased the fire hazard inside Command Module 012.
records.detail: The 1967 Review Board documented a 100 percent oxygen cabin atmosphere at 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute during the ground test, and determined that the test conditions were extremely hazardous. It also determined that this atmosphere presents severe fire hazards if the amount and location of combustibles in the Command Module are not restricted and controlled.
records.caution: Oxygen accelerated combustion; it was not itself the ignition spark.

image.alt: Apollo Command and Service Module 012 hanging from a crane above its adapter during preflight processing, with technicians working around it.
image.caption: Spacecraft 012 during preparations for the Apollo/Saturn 204 mission, January 1967. Processing photograph, not an image of the fire.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S67-15717; center JSC; record date 1967-01-03. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The test used a 16.7 psia, 100 percent oxygen atmosphere.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 2: "The test was conducted with a 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute, 100-percent oxygen atmosphere."

crosswalk.claim: The test conditions were extremely hazardous.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 2, Determination: "The test conditions were extremely hazardous."

crosswalk.claim: The atmosphere presents severe fire hazards if combustibles are not restricted and controlled.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 9, Determination: "This atmosphere presents severe fire hazards if the amount and location of combustibles in the Command Module are not restricted and controlled."

records.title: About fifteen seconds changed the system.
records.dek: The surviving instrument record describes an extraordinarily rapid pressure-and-fire sequence.
records.detail: The first fire transmission began at 23:31:04.7 GMT. About six seconds later the cabin-pressure sensor showed a clear rise; by about 23:31:16 its range was exceeded. The pressure vessel ruptured, at a pressure of at least 29 psia, at about 23:31:19 GMT. The Board describes the first stage of the fire as ending approximately 15 seconds after the verbal report. Counting from the 23:31:04.7 report to the 23:31:19.4 rupture mark gives 14.7 seconds. These are approximate marks from the Board account, not a reconstructed second-by-second animation.
records.caution: The timeline reports observed markers. The intervals between them are not interpolated sensor measurements.

image.alt: Astronaut Virgil Grissom stepping through a hatch into an altitude chamber while Roger Chaffee follows and Edward White stands with chamber technicians.
image.caption: The prime crew preparing to enter their spacecraft in the altitude chamber at Kennedy Space Center, 18 October 1966. Training photograph taken months before the fire.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S66-58038; center JSC; record date 1966-10-18. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The first verbal fire report began at 23:31:04.7 GMT.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V: "This transmission began at 23:31:04.7 GMT with an exclamatory remark."

crosswalk.claim: The first pressure increase was recorded about 6 seconds after the report.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V, Cabin Pressure Rise: "about 6 seconds after the crew first reported the fire". The NASA web text prints the clock time as 23:21:11, an apparent typographical error for 23:31:11; the interval is unaffected.

crosswalk.claim: Pressure exceeded the transducer range (17 psia cabin) by 23:31:16 GMT.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V, Cabin Pressure Rise.

crosswalk.claim: The cabin ruptured at about 23:31:19 GMT at a pressure of at least 29 psia.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V: "The cabin ruptured at a time of about 23:31:19 GMT and at a pressure of at least 29 psia."

crosswalk.claim: The first stage of the fire ended approximately 15 seconds after the verbal report.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V, Chronology of the Fire: the first stage "terminated approximately 15 seconds after the verbal report of fire". The interval between the 04.7 and 19.4 time marks is 14.7 seconds; this page uses the Board's wording, "about fifteen".

records.title: The hatch opened inward.
records.dek: The innermost hatch opened inward, and the Board found that, with the cabin pressurized, it could not be opened before rupture.
records.detail: NASA's history of the accident says the innermost of the command module's hatches opened inward and took 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions. The Review Board found that, due to internal pressure, the inner hatch could not be opened before the pressure vessel ruptured. Emergency procedures assigned the hatch to the Senior Pilot, Ed White. The Board found his harness buckle unopened after the fire, which indicated that he had begun the standard hatch-opening procedure.
records.caution: The hatch was one of several interacting hazards, not a standalone explanation of the fire.

image.alt: Display cases in a dimly lit museum gallery holding the sections of the three-part Apollo 1 hatch under the heading 'Portals into the Unknown'.
image.caption: The three-part hatch that was in place on the Apollo 1 spacecraft, displayed in the 2017 tribute at Kennedy Space Center's Apollo/Saturn V Center. A museum display photographed 24 January 2017.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0129; the record is the NASA Image Library detail page. NASA description: "The three-part hatch that was in place on the Apollo 1 spacecraft is shown in a tribute". Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.source: NASA History (2022): "with the innermost one opening inward and taking 90 seconds to open under ideal conditions".

crosswalk.claim: Due to internal pressure the inner hatch could not be opened before rupture.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 4: "Due to internal pressure, the Command Module inner hatch could not be opened prior to rupture of the Command Module."

crosswalk.claim: Ed White, as Senior Pilot, was responsible for opening the hatch in an emergency.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V: "Emergency procedures called for the Senior Pilot, occupying the center couch, to unlatch and remove the hatch". NASA crew biographies: "Ed White was selected as Senior Pilot for the first Apollo flight."

crosswalk.claim: The Senior Pilot's harness buckle was found unopened, indicating that he had begun the standard hatch-opening procedure.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Part V: "The Senior Pilot's harness buckle was found unopened after the fire indicating that he initiated the standard hatch opening procedure."

records.title: The spark was never conclusively identified.
records.dek: The Board determined that the most probable initiator was an electrical arc, and also found that no single ignition source was conclusively identified.
records.detail: The Apollo 204 Review Board determined that the most probable initiator of the fire was an electrical arc in the sector between the -Y and +Z spacecraft axes. It also found that no single ignition source was conclusively identified. The Board documented the extremely hazardous test conditions and the severe fire hazard of combustibles in that atmosphere, and determined that the crew was never capable of effecting emergency egress.
records.caution: Probable is not proven. This experience deliberately keeps the uncertainty visible.

image.alt: Close view of the charred interior of Apollo Command Module 012 at Pad 34 showing heavy heat and fire damage.
image.caption: Interior of Command Module 012 at Pad 34, photographed 28 January 1967, the day after the fire. No people are shown.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id S67-21294; center JSC; record date 1967-01-28. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: The Board determined that the most probable initiator was an electrical arc in the sector between the -Y and +Z spacecraft axes.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 1, Determination: "The most probable initiator was an electrical arc in the sector between -Y and +Z spacecraft axes."

crosswalk.claim: No single ignition source of the fire was conclusively identified.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 1: "No single ignition source of the fire was conclusively identified."

crosswalk.claim: The crew was never capable of effecting emergency egress.
crosswalk.source: Board report, Finding 4, Determination: "The crew was never capable of effecting emergency egress because of the pressurization before rupture and their loss of consciousness soon after rupture."

records.title: Inward became outward.
records.dek: NASA replaced the inward-opening hatch with a unified hatch that opened outward, from inside or outside, in three seconds.
records.detail: NASA's history of the accident describes a new unified, outward-opening hatch that could be opened from inside or outside the spacecraft in three seconds. NASA's history of the flammability tests records 102 deliberate ignitions of Command Module Boilerplate 1224 between December 1967 and February 1968, in three series of tests. Our reading: these tests show NASA examining how fire would actually behave rather than assuming it could always be prevented.
records.caution: The improvements were part of a broad redesign; Apollo 1 did not create every safety innovation from nothing.

image.alt: A lit museum display case holding a hatch, with on-image text stating the Block I hatch was designed to open in 90 seconds and the Block II hatch in 5 seconds.
image.caption: The redesigned hatch in the 2017 Apollo 1 tribute at Kennedy Space Center. The exhibit text states the Block I hatch was designed to open in 90 seconds and the Block II in 5. A museum display photographed 24 January 2017.
image.identity_note: NASA Image API nasa_id KSC-20170124-PH_KLS01_0090; NASA description: 'A redesigned hatch for an Apollo spacecraft is shown inside the new tribute'. Verified 2026-10-30.

crosswalk.claim: NASA replaced the inward-opening hatch with a unified hatch that opened outward and could be opened from inside or outside in three seconds.
crosswalk.source: NASA History (2022): "a unified hatch that could be opened from inside or outside the spacecraft in three seconds"; the astronauts cited "the new outward-opening unified hatch". Exhibit text photographed at Kennedy Space Center gives 5 seconds for the Block II hatch; this page uses NASA's article.

crosswalk.claim: 102 deliberate ignitions of Boilerplate 1224 between December 1967 and February 1968.
crosswalk.source: NASA History (2018): "three series of tests comprising 102 deliberate ignitions between December 1967 and February 1968".

chronology.unit: seconds after the first verbal fire report
chronology.notice: Only these four markers are documented in the Board account. The spaces between them are not sensor measurements and nothing is interpolated.

markers.label: First verbal report of fire
markers.note: The crew gave the first verbal indication of an emergency.

markers.label: First indication of a cabin pressure increase
markers.note: About 6 seconds after the report, per the Board account.

markers.label: Pressure exceeded the sensors' range
markers.note: The cabin transducer range was 17 psia; the battery compartment transducer range was 21 psia.

markers.label: Command Module pressure vessel ruptured
markers.note: At a pressure of at least 29 psia. The Board gives both 'about 23:31:19' and 23:31:19.4.
